accepted.question_text: What physical mechanism stabilizes an electron against Coulomb explosion when the electron is treated as a localized charged object, and can a quantitatively correct balance between its electromagnetic self-repulsion and the required non-electromagnetic counterforce also explain the observed value of the fine-structure constant α, the dimensionless electromagnetic coupling constant?

evidence.page: Section 1) The Stability of the Electron, opening paragraphs
evidence.quote: My longtime favorite is the puzzle about the internal stability of the electron, the prototype of all charged particles. If one considers a tiny charge cloud, it would explode due to electrostatic repulsion ("Coulomb explosion"). ... Balancing electromagnetic against non-electromagnetic forces might determine alpha and thereby solve both of these century-old problems in one stroke.

accepted.question_text: For an electron embedded in the Dirac sea, can one construct a complete local force-balance description that simultaneously accounts for vacuum polarization, the exchange hole produced by the exclusion principle, and the compensating exchange electron, so that the net forces on the reference electron and its surrounding exchange exciton are fully balanced in a mathematically controlled many-body quantum-electrodynamic treatment?

evidence.page: Section 1) The Stability of the Electron, subsection The Exchange Force
evidence.quote: After figuring out the exchange interaction in the Dirac sea, one can return to the original goal of balancing the forces acting on the reference electron, the exchange hole, and the exchange electron. This object resembles the negative ion of positronium, which has been investigated both theoretically and experimentally.

accepted.question_text: Can the Higgs sector of the standard model be replaced by a self-consistent composite Higgs description in which the Higgs boson is built from scalar pairs of electroweak gauge bosons such as WW and ZZ, with gauge-boson self-interactions generating the effective quadratic and quartic terms needed to break weak symmetry, reproduce the observed Higgs mass and vacuum expectation value with fewer adjustable parameters, and predict experimentally testable resonances in gauge-boson scattering near the Higgs-pair threshold?

evidence.page: Section 2) A Higgs Boson Composed of Gauge Bosons
evidence.quote: If the resulting gauge boson potential breaks the weak symmetry, the proposed model would become self-consistent and yield a new standard model with fewer adjustable parameters. ... It would be particularly interesting to look for resonances in elastic gauge boson scattering, caused by an intermediate Higgs pair. Combining precision measurements of the Higgs mass with calculations beyond the leading order should enable a critical test against other models for the Higgs boson.

accepted.question_text: Can one formulate a relativistic classical and quantum field-theoretic expansion in terms of interacting anharmonic waves, rather than non-interacting sinusoidal modes, in a way that remains compatible with the basic requirements of relativity and quantum physics despite abandoning familiar structures such as linear superposition, orthogonality, and single-particle eigenstates, and can such a framework usefully describe intrinsically nonlinear phenomena such as strong-field laser processes, nuclear strong-interaction effects, or gravitational-wave emission from black holes?

evidence.page: Section 3) Anharmonic Waves in (Quantum) Field Theory, opening paragraphs
evidence.quote: Nevertheless, classical and quantum fields are typically expanded into non-interacting sinusoidal waves when describing scattering. Would it be possible to develop an expansion into a more general class of interacting waves? What are the criteria for such waves to satisfy basic priciples of physics?
